title: You Think Brain Cells Only Wire Together, Yet Firing Late Actually Weakens the Link
description:
Clinical Case Briefing — Donald Hebb (1949) & Bliss and Lømo (1973): 'Cells That Fire Together, Wire Together' — From Bold Guess to LTP Proof, grounded in D.O. Hebb (2005) (The Organization of Behavior). Empirical findings show that in 1949, four years BEFORE electron microscopes had even photographed a synaptic cleft clearly, McGill psychologist Donald O. Hebb wrote 67 words on page 62 of The Organization of Behavior that became the most influential sentence in brain science:.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how auditory cortex, hippocampus, prefrontal cortex coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that 'When an axon of cell A is near enough to excite a cell B and repeatedly or persistently takes part in firing it, some growth process or metabolic change takes place in one or both cells such that A's efficiency, as one of the cells firing B, is increased' — immortalized in 6 crisp words by Stanford neurobiologist Carla Shatz (1992): 'Cells that fire together, wire together!'.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- D.O. Hebb (2005). The Organization of Behavior. https://doi.org/10.4324/9781410612403
- T. V. P. Bliss, Terje Lømo (1973). Long-lasting potentiation of synaptic transmission in the dentate area of the anaesthetized rabbit following stimulation of the perforant path. The Journal of Physiology. https://doi.org/10.1113/jphysiol.1973.sp010273
- Jungwoo Kang (2016). Historical figures in neuroscience: Donald Hebb. Cambridge Medicine Journal. https://doi.org/10.7244/cmj.2016.02.002

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.
